newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK unemployment at six-year low, wages surge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK unemployment at six-year low, wages surge.

text.p: Britain's unemployment rate fell to a six-year low of 6.2 percent in February, providing a welcome boost for the embattled Conservative government as it started an election campaign well behind in opinion polls.

But the good news for Prime Minister John Major was tempered by a surge in retail sales and an unexpected jump in average earnings, which suggested inflationary pressures are building and interest rates may need to rise soon after the May 1 election.

This will provide ammunition for the opposition Labour party to challenge the key plank of Major's election campaign -- that he has delivered an unrivalled combination of steady growth, low inflation and falling unemployment.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Wednesday that unemployment fell 68,200 in February to 1.75 million, representing 6.2 percent of the workforce. It was the lowest total jobless figure since October 1990 and the 12th consecutive monthly fall.
Major, whose party is around 25 points behind Labour in opinion polls, said the drop in unemployment was proof that Britain was booming.
"Falling unemployment, stable prices, lower taxes, higher living standards -- people's hard work has created a turbo-economy, which is making life better right across the country," he said.
His deputy Michael Heseltine said Britain's record of falling unemployment was due to its flexible labour market and its refusal to sign up to the European Union's Social Chapter on workers' rights.

"Even our worst regions now have unemployment comparable with Germany's best," he told a news conference. "Fundamental to our success is the opt-out from the Social Chapter. If our success is to be maintained, that opt-out must be maintained."

However, Labour dismissed the figures as "fantasy" and said they had been "fiddled" as they reflect the number of people allowed to claim unemployment benefit rather than those who want a job but cannot find one.

"I don't believe most people think the statistics are a true reflection of the situation," Labour leader Tony Blair told reporters in Birmingham. "Many people are not eligible to claim unemployment benefit but are still basically unemployed,"
Retail sales, a key barometer of consumer confidence, rose a stronger than expected 0.5 percent in February and were up 4.4 percent year-on-year.
Average earnings rose five percent in January, the highest increase since November 1992.

Economists said the two sets of figures suggested the British economy might be steaming ahead too fast and that the next government, of whichever party, will have to raise interest rates from their present 6.0 percent.

Bank of England Governor Eddie George recommended raising interest rates to 6.25 percent at his monetary meeting with finance minister Kenneth Clarke on February 5, according to minutes of the meeting published on Wednesday.
George warned that the government was unlikely to meet his 2.5 percent inflation target.
But Major said on Wednesday that inflation would probably fall further.
"We have actually got a low inflation economy in this country and it looks as though inflation will go lower still," he said. "If we stick to the broad policies we have followed, it will stay low."
